                Ms
                Meta · featured social app

                Facebook Messenger: the complete connection guide

                Messenger brings one-to-one chats, group conversations, calls, personalization, quick reactions, disappearing-message controls, Meta AI, and buyer-seller conversations together. Use the card above to rate it, vote it a favorite, save it to your wishlist, or compare it with another app.

                Chats & shared media

                Send text, photos, videos, links, GIFs, stickers, files, and voice notes. Reply to a specific message and revisit the conversation’s shared media when you need to find something again.

                Voice calls

                Start an internet voice call from an eligible one-to-one or group chat. Mute the microphone, switch audio output, and use headphones when you want more privacy.

                Video calls

                Turn on face-to-face video, flip cameras, mute, and move between voice and video controls. A quick camera-and-microphone check avoids surprises before an important call.

                Group chats

                Gather family, friends, or project teams in one thread. Give the chat a clear name, use direct replies, manage notifications, and start group voice or video calls when available.

                Chat themes & nicknames

                Personalize supported conversations with a theme, color, emoji, and nicknames. These settings help chats feel distinct, but they do not change your whole phone’s appearance.

                Reactions & replies

                React to a message for a fast acknowledgment, or reply directly when several topics are moving at once. This keeps busy group chats easier to follow.

                Vanish mode & disappearing controls

                Where available, disappearing-message features remove eligible messages after the conditions shown in the chat are met. Treat them as convenience, not guaranteed secrecy—someone can still save or capture what they see.

                Meta AI inside Messenger

                In supported accounts and regions, chat with Meta AI for brainstorming, explanations, planning, or creative prompts, and bring it into eligible conversations. Check important answers because AI can be incomplete or wrong.

                Marketplace chats

                Facebook Marketplace conversations can open a buyer-seller thread in Messenger, keeping questions about the item together. Keep payment and pickup decisions cautious, and watch for pressure to leave the platform.

                Privacy, requests & notifications

                Review message requests before replying, mute noisy threads, control who can reach you, and use block or report tools when something feels wrong. Settings and labels can vary by device and version.

                Messenger pro tips

                • Use search inside a conversation instead of endlessly scrolling for an old name, phrase, or link.
                • Reply to the exact message in a fast group chat so everyone knows what you mean.
                • Mute, do not abandon: quiet a busy thread for a chosen period while keeping the conversation available.
                • Check before calling: confirm microphone, camera, speaker, connection, and who is in the chat.
                • Protect your account: use a unique password, turn on two-factor authentication, and review unfamiliar login alerts.
                • Be selective with AI: do not paste passwords, financial details, medical records, private messages, or another person’s personal information into Meta AI.
                • Shop safely: inspect the listing and seller profile, avoid pressure or unusual payment requests, and meet in a public place when an in-person exchange is appropriate.
                • Keep context together: use one Marketplace thread per listing and one clearly named group per project.

                Messenger fun facts

                • Messenger grew out of Facebook’s original built-in chat and later became a standalone app.
                • A reaction works like a tiny visual reply, making it useful when a full message would interrupt the flow.
                • Chat themes can give different conversations their own look without changing every chat.
                • Group chats can combine conversation, media sharing, direct replies, and group calling in one thread.
                • Marketplace messaging keeps the listing conversation connected to the people discussing it.
                • Meta AI turns Messenger into both a people-to-people chat space and, where available, an AI conversation space.

                Feature names and availability can vary by account, region, device, age eligibility, and app version. Always follow the controls shown in your own chat.

                Did you know? Software history shelf

                From boxes to downloads

                Computer software once commonly arrived on floppy disks and CDs. App stores and browser-based tools later made installing and updating software much more direct.

                Chat became multimedia

                Early online chat centered on typed text. Modern messaging added photos, voice notes, reactions, group calls, themes, and AI-assisted conversations.

                Files learned to travel

                Cloud storage changed the routine from carrying one physical copy to opening synchronized files across phones, tablets, and computers.

                Skype became software history

                Skype helped make internet calling familiar worldwide. Microsoft retired the consumer Skype service in 2025 and directed people toward Microsoft Teams.

                Fun software facts

                • Apps keep evolving: updates can add tools, redesign menus, or change how a feature works.
                • Creative workflows can mix: one idea may move from notes to design to video before it is ready to share.
                • Your rating is personal: five stars can mean relaxing, useful, funny, powerful—or simply perfect for you.

                Smart app tips

                1. Check permissions: give an app only the camera, microphone, photos, or location access it actually needs.
                2. Use official app stores: read the developer name and recent reviews before downloading.
                3. Protect your creations: keep important originals backed up before editing or replacing them.
                4. Try one feature at a time: a short test project makes a big app feel much easier to learn.

                  Picnic among the stars

                  Hazza has the star map. DJ Malik has the moon bass. Angel panda packed enough snacks for three galaxies. Snuggle bug brought the emergency blankets. boo bear is staring down the space grumps. Tigger is bouncing through zero gravity, and Grogu is already taste-testing the cargo.

                  Pack the rocket basket

                  The Great Zero-Gravity Picnic

                  Mama Christina called, “Plushies, launch in five!” and the whole family tumbled into the cuddle rocket. Hazza took the navigator’s chair and threaded the ship between glittering comet tails. DJ Malik turned the cockpit into a space DJ set, mixing rocket hums with a bass line that made Saturn’s rings wobble.

                  Angel panda ran comfort-and-snack duty, passing out star sandwiches and calm hugs whenever the ship bumped. Snuggle bug tucked everyone beneath one enormous cosmic quilt so no tiny paws or ears got chilly. When a cloud of grumpy space grumps drifted toward the picnic blanket, boo bear stood guard and stared them down until they apologized and offered moon crackers.

                  Then Tigger bounced from crater to crater—because bouncing is what Tiggers do best!—while Grogu, the very serious chief snack-taster, sampled every zero-gravity bite twice “for quality control.” Under a sky full of gold and pink stars, all seven plushies raised their juice boxes to Mama and declared the first family space picnic a glorious, crumb-filled success.

                  Hub 122 · clear facts, calm support

                  ✚ Diabetes & Pregnancy: Know the Risks

                  Diabetes in pregnancy can mean type 1 or type 2 diabetes that was present before pregnancy, or gestational diabetes first diagnosed during pregnancy. The risks are not identical for every person, and having a risk does not mean a complication will happen.

                  Before pregnancyThe three typesRisksWarning signsMonitoring & birthAfter birthSupportMedical advice & sources
                  FACTUAL HEALTH INFORMATION

                  Knowledge can help you ask better questions.

                  Blood sugar that stays above the recommended range can raise the chance of complications. Good care before, during, and after pregnancy can lower many of these risks.

                  Important difference: birth-defect risk is especially linked with pre-existing diabetes and high blood sugar around conception and early pregnancy. Gestational diabetes usually develops later, after the baby’s organs have formed.

                  ✚

                  Before pregnancy: plan early when you can

                  The earliest weeks matter—often before someone knows they are pregnant. Bringing glucose as close as safely possible to the personal range set by a clinician before conception can lower the chance of miscarriage and major birth defects.

                  Build the care team

                  Plan with an OB-GYN or maternal-fetal medicine specialist and a diabetes clinician. They can review glucose goals, diabetes technology, kidney and eye health, and other conditions.

                  Check folic acid

                  A higher-dose folic acid supplement is often discussed for people with pre-existing diabetes before conception and in early pregnancy. The right dose varies, so ask the care team rather than choosing one alone.

                  Review every medicine

                  Some blood-pressure and cholesterol medicines—and other prescription, over-the-counter, or herbal products—may need to be changed before or during pregnancy. Do not stop anything on your own; review the full list with a clinician.

                  No perfect timing? If pregnancy has already started, contact the care team promptly. Support and safer planning can begin now—this is about care, not blame.

                  The three types are not the same

                  All three can raise pregnancy risks when glucose is above the recommended range, but timing and treatment needs differ.

                  Type 1 diabetes

                  The body makes little or no insulin, so insulin is essential. Insulin needs can change quickly during pregnancy, and the risks tied to high glucose begin around conception. There is also a greater concern for diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).

                  Type 2 diabetes

                  The body does not use insulin well and may not make enough. It is present before pregnancy, so glucose around conception matters. Medicines, blood pressure, and existing kidney, eye, heart, or nerve conditions may need review.

                  Gestational diabetes

                  This first develops during pregnancy, usually later than the organ-forming weeks. Birth-defect risk is therefore different from pre-existing diabetes, but high glucose can still raise the chance of a large baby, birth complications, newborn low blood sugar, and future type 2 diabetes for parent and child.

                  Maternal risks

                  Possible complications for the pregnant person include:

                  High blood pressure and preeclampsia

                  Diabetes raises the chance of pregnancy-related high blood pressure, including preeclampsia.

                  Cesarean birth and difficult delivery

                  A larger baby can make labor and vaginal delivery harder and can increase the chance of a C-section or birth-related injury.

                  Preterm labor or birth

                  Labor may begin early, or the medical team may recommend an earlier delivery because of complications.

                  Infections

                  Bladder and other infections can be more common when diabetes is not well controlled.

                  Existing diabetes complications may worsen

                  With diabetes that predates pregnancy, existing eye, kidney, heart, or nerve problems can worsen and may need closer monitoring.

                  Future type 2 diabetes after gestational diabetes

                  After gestational diabetes, the parent has a higher lifetime risk of developing type 2 diabetes and needs follow-up testing.

                  Baby, fetal, and newborn risks

                  Possible risks during pregnancy, birth, or the newborn period include:

                  Birth defects

                  High blood sugar around conception and early pregnancy can raise the risk of major birth defects, especially with pre-existing type 1 or type 2 diabetes.

                  Miscarriage or stillbirth

                  Poorly controlled diabetes can raise the risk of pregnancy loss or stillbirth.

                  Very large baby

                  Extra glucose can make the baby grow larger than expected. This can lead to shoulder problems, nerve injury, or a broken collarbone during a difficult birth.

                  Preterm birth and breathing problems

                  The baby may be born early and may have trouble breathing, especially when the lungs have not fully matured.

                  Low blood sugar after birth

                  A newborn may have hypoglycemia soon after delivery and may need prompt feeding, glucose, and monitoring.

                  Jaundice

                  The newborn can have a higher chance of jaundice, which causes yellowing of the skin and eyes and may need treatment.

                  Long-term risks for the child

                  Children exposed to high blood sugar during pregnancy have a higher chance of:

                  Overweight or obesity

                  The risk is higher later in childhood and adolescence, although many other health, family, and environmental factors also matter.

                  Type 2 diabetes

                  The child has a higher chance of developing type 2 diabetes later in life. This is increased risk, not a prediction of what will happen to one child.

                  Warning signs: get help now

                  Pregnant and experiencing any of the signs below? Contact the maternity or diabetes team immediately. For severe symptoms, trouble staying awake, trouble breathing, or when the care team cannot be reached promptly, call emergency services or go to the emergency department.

                  • Possible preeclampsiaSevere or persistent headache, vision changes, sudden swelling—especially of the face or hands—or pain high in the belly, particularly on the right side.
                  • Possible diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)Nausea or vomiting, belly pain, fruity-smelling breath, rapid or deep breathing, unusual sleepiness, or confusion. DKA can become dangerous quickly and may happen at lower glucose levels during pregnancy.
                  • Decreased fetal movementA clear decrease or change in the baby’s usual movement pattern needs prompt advice from the maternity team. Do not wait until the next appointment.

                  This is not a complete emergency list. Trust your instincts: if something feels seriously wrong, seek urgent care.

                  Extra monitoring and delivery planning

                  More appointments do not mean something is already wrong. They help the team notice changes early and choose the safest plan.

                  Glucose and parent health

                  The team may review glucose readings more often and follow blood pressure, urine, medicines, nutrition, and diabetes-related eye or kidney health.

                  Baby’s growth and wellbeing

                  Extra ultrasounds may check anatomy, growth, and amniotic fluid. Growth scans, non-stress tests, or other fetal-wellbeing checks may be offered depending on the diabetes type, glucose levels, medicines, and other risks.

                  A flexible birth plan

                  Timing depends on glucose control, fetal growth, blood pressure, medicines, and complications. Earlier delivery is sometimes discussed when continuing the pregnancy may be less safe. If the baby is very large, the team may discuss C-section because of shoulder and birth-injury concerns; it is not automatic for everyone.

                  There is no one-size-fits-all testing or delivery schedule. Ask what is being recommended, why, and what would change the plan.

                  After birth: glucose, feeding, and follow-up

                  Birth changes insulin needs quickly, and postpartum care matters for both parent and baby.

                  Glucose can swing

                  Insulin needs often drop sharply after the placenta is delivered, so low blood sugar can happen—especially with insulin, disrupted meals, and feeding a newborn. The diabetes team should guide medication changes.

                  Breastfeeding support

                  Breastfeeding can benefit parent and baby and may support healthier long-term metabolism. Diabetes does not automatically prevent breastfeeding, but glucose management, medicines, feeding support, and the baby’s needs should be discussed with the care team.

                  Keep the follow-up

                  Babies may have glucose checked after birth. People who had gestational diabetes need postpartum diabetes testing and ongoing screening; people with type 1 or type 2 diabetes need their management plan reviewed after delivery.

                  Mind, heart, partner, and family

                  A high-risk label can bring stress, worry, guilt, or information overload. None of that means someone has failed.

                  Be on your own side

                  Glucose numbers are information, not a grade. Self-compassion, rest, and honest conversations can make a demanding care plan feel more manageable.

                  Ask for emotional support

                  Tell the care team about persistent anxiety, sadness, panic, or feeling unable to cope. Counseling, peer groups, diabetes educators, and perinatal mental-health support can help.

                  How loved ones can help

                  Offer rides to appointments, learn the urgent warning signs, help with meals or supplies, listen without policing glucose numbers, celebrate effort, and ask what support is wanted today.

                  Please talk with a doctor for personal medical advice

                  This hub is general education—not a diagnosis, emergency assessment, or personal treatment plan. An OB-GYN, midwife, maternal-fetal medicine specialist, diabetes clinician, pharmacist, or other qualified professional can explain which risks apply, set safe blood-sugar goals, review every medicine and supplement, choose a folic acid dose, and plan monitoring, birth, feeding, and postpartum care.

                  A healthy pregnancy is possible. Planning when possible, keeping prenatal appointments, following the individual care plan, and getting recommended follow-up after birth can reduce risk. Never start, stop, or change insulin or another medicine based on this page.

                  CDC: Diabetes During Pregnancy ↗CDC: Gestational Diabetes ↗NIDDK: Long-Term Effects ↗CDC: Pre-Existing Diabetes Fact Sheet ↗ADA: Gestational Diabetes Guide ↗

                  🌙 Moonlit Healing Hands

                  A gentle moonlit space for comforting rituals, reflective moon moods, creative light, and calm companionship. Nothing here diagnoses or treats anything; it simply offers cozy pauses you can choose, change, or stop.

                  EntranceCalm ritualBreatheVisualizeMoon moodsSky mixerSend lightGuardiansJournal
                  the night is quiet enough for you

                  Step into the moonlight.

                  You do not have to fix the whole day tonight. Set down one heavy thought, unclench one small place, and let the silver glow meet you exactly where you are.

                  angel panda saved the softest patch of moonlight for you.

                  Round one · crisp & cool

                  Round two · toastable comfort

                  India · masala toast-inspired triangles

                  Toast topped with mashed potato, peas, lemon, and a gentle spice blend.

                  There is room for two favorites.

                  Allergy & hygiene check: read every label; sesame, milk, and wheat appear in this tasting set. Use clean utensils for each snack, wash produce, and keep chilled ingredients cold until serving.

                  Choose a calm-moment pairing. “Healing Bites” is a cozy ritual name only—food and tea are not medical treatment and make no health promises.

                  Warm cinnamon apple cup

                  Microwave diced apple with a spoonful of water in short bursts until soft, then add cinnamon and oats. Let it cool before tasting.

                  Check the temperature carefully. Oats may contain gluten unless labeled gluten-free.

                  🎭 Dramatic Readings Theater

                  Take the most ordinary words in the house, hand them an imaginary spotlight, and perform them like the fate of snack time depends on it.

                  The stagePerformance voicesScript libraryLaugh-O-MeterFilm your reading

                  Ordinary words. Outrageous delivery.

                  Dramatic Readings Theater 🎭

                  Tonight: the grocery list. Tomorrow: the laundry instructions. NO text is safe!

                  ◖ ◗HOUSE LIGHTS DOWN!onedirectionhealinghq

                  Pick Your Performance Voice

                  Tap a voice, square your shoulders, and give the cereal box the performance it deserves.

                  The Script Library

                  Tap any card to make it tonight’s feature presentation. Stage directions are mandatory-ish.

                  The Grocery List

                  [Enter as if returning from a terrible voyage.] Milk. Eggs. Bread. Three brave staples, united by destiny.

                  [Freeze. Search the list.] But where is the cheese? WHERE IS THE CHEESE?

                  [Turn slowly toward an imaginary camera.] We trusted this list. It betrayed us.

                  Laundry Instructions

                  [Hold the care label toward the light.] Cold wash. Gentle cycle. No bleach. These are not suggestions. They are a prophecy.

                  [Lift a dryer sheet like a love letter.] Dearest sheet, you made every sock softer. Meet me beyond the lint trap.

                  [Bow to the washing machine.] Spin wisely, noble drum.

                  The Wi-Fi Password

                  [Check both hallways. Lower your voice.] The code is... Capital P. Lowercase l. The number seven. Underscore.

                  [Lean closer.] Repeat it to no one. Write it on nothing.

                  [Long pause.] Also, that might be a one, not a lowercase L. Our mission is compromised.

                  The Weather Report

                  [Stare accusingly at the sky.] Today brings clouds. Again. As though yesterday’s clouds were not enough.

                  [Open an umbrella with wounded dignity.] A thirty-percent chance of rain? Make up your mind, atmosphere!

                  [Point toward the horizon.] Tomorrow: sunshine. Allegedly.

                  Kiki's Catchphrases

                  [Step into the spotlight.] “No limits just fun!”

                  [Sweep one arm toward the exit.] “Yeet the negativity!”

                  [Repeat both lines in your chosen voice, then accept a standing ovation from every pillow in the room.]

                  Tonight’s comboMovie Trailer Guy performs The Grocery List.
